results.title: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity coflow flames contain five to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal-gravity flames.
results.claim: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity coflow flames contain five to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal-gravity flames.
results.quote: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity ﬂames contain ﬁve to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal gravity ﬂames.

results.title: When the fuel is diluted with nitrogen the soot disappears and the flame can lift off the burner and appear as a faint blue cone; with more dilution it becomes a flat disk and finally extinguishes.
results.claim: When the fuel is diluted with nitrogen the soot disappears and the flame can lift off the burner and appear as a faint blue cone; with more dilution it becomes a flat disk and finally extinguishes.
results.quote: When the fuel is diluted with an inert gas (nitrogen in our case), the soot disappears and the ﬂame can lift oﬀ the burner surface and appear as a faint blue cone. With increased dilution, the ﬂame becomes a ﬂat disk, and ﬁnally extinguishes.

results.title: FLEX led to the discovery of a cool flame: the fuel kept burning under certain conditions after the visible flame went out.
results.claim: FLEX led to the discovery of a cool flame: the fuel kept burning under certain conditions after the visible flame went out.
results.quote: FLEX, which analyzed the effectiveness of fire suppressants, led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued "burning" under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.

results.title: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity on the BRE burner: soot appeared only at ignition and disappeared quickly.
results.claim: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity on the BRE burner: soot appeared only at ignition and disappeared quickly.
results.quote: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions, did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred upon ignition and disappeared quickly after ignition.

results.title: In a BRE test video the soot seen at ignition quickly fades away and leaves a dim blue flame.
results.claim: In a BRE test video the soot seen at ignition quickly fades away and leaves a dim blue flame.
results.quote: Initially, the flame behavior is similar to previous BRE tests. The flame is very sooty at ignition, due to ethylene's double bond, where you can see the glowing soot particles pass through the flame. But the soot quickly fades away leaving a dim blue flame, where blue is the natural color of hydrocarbon flames.

results.title: Sooting is far more significant in microgravity flames than in similar conditions with 1-g flames.
results.claim: Sooting is far more significant in microgravity flames than in similar conditions with 1-g flames.
results.quote: Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar conditions with 1-g flames.

results.title: In microgravity the voltage-current curve shows no distinctive saturation plateau; the flames show a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.
results.claim: In microgravity the voltage-current curve shows no distinctive saturation plateau; the flames show a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.
results.quote: The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.

results.title: The E-FIELD Flames report finds correlations between luminosity, combustion intensity and ion current, and suggests that the most robust burning produces the highest ion current even when the flame is most compact.
results.claim: The E-FIELD Flames report finds correlations between luminosity, combustion intensity and ion current, and suggests that the most robust burning produces the highest ion current even when the flame is most compact.
results.quote: There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current. The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even though the flame is most compact.

results.title: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity in s-Flame; soot appeared only during forced ignition from the hot wire and soon dissipated.
results.claim: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity in s-Flame; soot appeared only during forced ignition from the hot wire and soon dissipated.
results.quote: Ethylene flames which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred during forced ignition from the hotwire, but soon dissipated.

results.title: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength or combustion intensity.
results.claim: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength or combustion intensity.
results.quote: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).

results.title: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames were very faint and barely visible, but thermocouples, radiometers and photomultiplier tubes made their presence obvious.
results.claim: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames were very faint and barely visible, but thermocouples, radiometers and photomultiplier tubes made their presence obvious.
results.quote: These tests were conducted with nitrogen-diluted hydrogen fuel making the flames very faint. Even though the flames were barely visible, their presence was obvious due to the measurements of various instrumentation, including thermocouples, radiometers, and photomultiplier tubes.

results.title: Pure and diluted hydrogen flames were not apparent or hardly visible to the main data camera and the analog operations camera.
results.claim: Pure and diluted hydrogen flames were not apparent or hardly visible to the main data camera and the analog operations camera.
results.quote: A critical challenge for s-Flame was in imaging the pure hydrogen and diluted hydrogen flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the DataCam and analog operations camera.

results.title: CFI-G observed spherical non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuels for the first time.
results.claim: CFI-G observed spherical non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuels for the first time.
results.quote: New research conducted aboard the orbiting laboratory in June 2021 has now achieved another first for microgravity flame research. Data from tests conducted for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G), sponsored by the ISS U.S. National Lab and National Science Foundation, show the presence of cool flames. While the flames created aboard station in 2012 burned liquid fuel, these new cool flames burned gaseous fuels. This was the first time spherical non-premixed cool flames have been observed burning gaseous fuels.

results.title: Because cool flames give off little heat or light, they were too faint to be visible in real time during station testing; three cool flames were found afterwards in the thermal radiation and burner temperature data.
results.claim: Because cool flames give off little heat or light, they were too faint to be visible in real time during station testing; three cool flames were found afterwards in the thermal radiation and burner temperature data.
results.quote: Since cool flames give off little heat or light, they were too faint to be visible in real time during space station testing. The research team uncovered the presence of three cool flames in the data on thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after the hot flames were quenched.

results.title: As the opposed flow was gradually reduced, the thin-film flame shrank, lost its orange color and became completely blue.
results.claim: As the opposed flow was gradually reduced, the thin-film flame shrank, lost its orange color and became completely blue.
results.quote: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.

results.title: Just before quenching the rod flame shrank to a hemispherical blue shape, and pre-quenching oscillations at 1.1 Hz were observed with a radiometer.
results.claim: Just before quenching the rod flame shrank to a hemispherical blue shape, and pre-quenching oscillations at 1.1 Hz were observed with a radiometer.
results.quote: The flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue shape just before quenching. Prequenching extinction oscillations at 1.1 Hz are observed with a radiometer and are similar to previously reported quiescent candle flame oscillations in microgravity.

results.title: In the concurrent rod tests CO production increased significantly at low O2 levels, and so did the CO to CO2 ratio.
results.claim: In the concurrent rod tests CO production increased significantly at low O2 levels, and so did the CO to CO2 ratio.
results.quote: CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels. The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations.

results.title: At very low flow velocities the rod flames appeared very small, blue, faint and open at their downstream ends; as flow rose toward 20 mm/s and above they became much more luminous, with bright yellow flames.
results.claim: At very low flow velocities the rod flames appeared very small, blue, faint and open at their downstream ends; as flow rose toward 20 mm/s and above they became much more luminous, with bright yellow flames.
results.quote: Visually it was observed that at very low flow velocities the flames appear to be very small, blue, faint, and open at their downstream ends. As the flow velocity rises towards 20 mm/s and above, the flames become much more luminous, with bright yellow flames, and a closed downstream tip.

results.title: CO to CO2 ratios for the BASS-II fires were an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases.
results.claim: CO to CO2 ratios for the BASS-II fires were an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases.
results.quote: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.

results.title: Concurrent-flow PMMA rod flames produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
results.claim: Concurrent-flow PMMA rod flames produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
results.quote: Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.

results.title: In general the BASS-II flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel: some ended up as soot, some as CO and some as unburned hydrocarbons.
results.claim: In general the BASS-II flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel: some ended up as soot, some as CO and some as unburned hydrocarbons.
results.quote: So, in general, the flames were under- ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel. Some fuel ended up as soot, some as CO, and some as unburned hydrocarbons.

results.title: The FLEX series showed that quasi-steady stable flames can surround a droplet in microgravity without a visible flame, at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike hot flames, whose temperature is higher than 1200 K.
results.claim: The FLEX series showed that quasi-steady stable flames can surround a droplet in microgravity without a visible flame, at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike hot flames, whose temperature is higher than 1200 K.
results.quote: FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K.

results.title: In CFI, warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and were not visible in the color camera; subsequently a hot flame ignited and quickly extinguished to form a cool flame.
results.claim: In CFI, warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and were not visible in the color camera; subsequently a hot flame ignited and quickly extinguished to form a cool flame.
results.quote: Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera. Subsequently, a hot flame is ignited which quickly extinguishes to form a cool flame.

results.title: In CFI, at low pressures soot is not formed in the cool flame because of its low flame temperature, and soot formed during the hot flame is simply convected away from the droplet surface; when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after hot flame extinction.
results.claim: In CFI, at low pressures soot is not formed in the cool flame because of its low flame temperature, and soot formed during the hot flame is simply convected away from the droplet surface; when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after hot flame extinction.
results.quote: At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction. The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis and research is needed.
